blocks.raw: ## Updates to V4 Open Banking API
blocks.text: Updates to V4 Open Banking API

blocks.raw: In June 2024, the Open Banking Implementation Entity released **Version 4 of the Open Banking API standards**, with a mandate for CMA9 banks to begin migration. As the ecosystem evolves, we want to keep you informed about what this means for your integration with Modulr Payment Initiation Services.
blocks.text: In June 2024, the Open Banking Implementation Entity released Version 4 of the Open Banking API standards, with a mandate for CMA9 banks to begin migration. As the ecosystem evolves, we want to keep you informed about what this means for your integration with Modulr Payment Initiation Services.

blocks.raw: ✅ **What’s changing?**
blocks.text: ✅ What’s changing?

blocks.raw: While the technical updates in Open Banking V4 **do not impact existing Modulr client integrations**, there are a few key enhancements worth noting for future:
blocks.text: While the technical updates in Open Banking V4 do not impact existing Modulr client integrations, there are a few key enhancements worth noting for future:

blocks.raw:
* **Improved Payment Statuses:** V4 introduces **more granular payment statuses**, offering better visibility into the lifecycle of a payment. While not mandatory, we recommend adopting these new codes to enhance your payment tracking and reconciliation processes.
* Updates apply to both **single immediate payments** and **fixed recurring payments (standing orders).** Some older status codes are being deprecated, and new ones are being introduced with clearer descriptions.
* **New Payment Context Codes** (non mandatory fields): new codes that you are able to adopt as an option.

blocks.raw: **🚀 HSBC first to deprecate Open Banking V3**
blocks.text: 🚀 HSBC first to deprecate Open Banking V3

blocks.raw: We’re pleased to share that **HSBC** is the first bank to remove V3 support for its Personal, Business & First Direct brands. This means it is now supporting Open Banking V4 requests only, returning additional payment status where applicable.  Other ASPSPs expected to follow, the next being Lloyds Bank with an expected November date.

This means it is now supporting Open Banking V4 requests only, returning additional payment status where applicable.  Other ASPSPs expected to follow, the next being Lloyds Bank with an expected November date.

blocks.raw: 🔄 **Backward compatibility**
blocks.text: 🔄 Backward compatibility

blocks.raw: There is **no confirmed deprecation date** for V3.1 long lived consents at this time. However, several ASPSPs (e.g. HSBC) have indicated that **existing V3.1 consents will remain valid under V4.** This means you can continue to use your existing consents without disrupting the current experience.

blocks.raw: ## 🔍 Coming soon - Verification of Payee (VoP) for SEPA payments
blocks.text: 🔍 Coming soon - Verification of Payee (VoP) for SEPA payments

blocks.raw: With the EU’s Verification of Payee planned deadline for Euro area financial institutions to participate by **9 October 2025**, we’re building the tools to help you stay compliant.
blocks.text: With the EU’s Verification of Payee planned deadline for Euro area financial institutions to participate by 9 October 2025, we’re building the tools to help you stay compliant.

blocks.raw:
🧭 **What’s driving this?**\
The EU’s Instant Payments Regulation (IPR) brings in a number of changes designed to drive the adoption of SEPA payments by consumers, businesses & financial institutions. A key change is the mandatory introduction of an account name checking service (VoP) for all Euro area financial institutions; a notable difference to other schemes is that it requires a name check on **every payment**, not just the first time a beneficiary is set up.
blocks.text: 🧭 What’s driving this?The EU’s Instant Payments Regulation (IPR) brings in a number of changes designed to drive the adoption of SEPA payments by consumers, businesses & financial institutions. A key change is the mandatory introduction of an account name checking service (VoP) for all Euro area financial institutions; a notable difference to other schemes is that it requires a name check on every payment, not just the first time a beneficiary is set up.

blocks.raw: **There will be no additional charge for partners and clients** - in line with regulatory requirements, the name check does not incur any further cost to the end user (PSU).
blocks.text: There will be no additional charge for partners and clients - in line with regulatory requirements, the name check does not incur any further cost to the end user (PSU).

blocks.raw:
🛠️ **What is Modulr doing?**\
We’re implementing our VoP service to support SEPA Payments with delivery expected in line with current industry timelines. Here’s what to expect:

blocks.raw: Outgoing payments to a Euro-area account: Modulr will provide a specific VoP API for name checks you can use before initiating a payment. This will be a non-breaking additional API endpoint, separate from the existing payment API.

blocks.raw: ## New Corporate Fraud Law: What You Need to Know Before 1 September 2025
blocks.text: New Corporate Fraud Law: What You Need to Know Before 1 September 2025

blocks.raw: From 1 September 2025, a major change in UK corporate law will come into effect: the “Failure to Prevent Fraud” offence, introduced under the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA).
blocks.text: From 1 September 2025, a major change in UK corporate law will come into effect: the “Failure to Prevent Fraud” offence, introduced under the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA).

blocks.raw: ⚖️ **What’s Changing?**
blocks.text: ⚖️ What’s Changing?

blocks.raw: Large organisations will be criminally liable if an employee, agent, subsidiary, or other “associated person” commits fraud for the organisation’s benefit—even if senior leadership was unaware of the wrongdoing.
blocks.text: Large organisations will be criminally liable if an employee, agent, subsidiary, or other “associated person” commits fraud for the organisation’s benefit—even if senior leadership was unaware of the wrongdoing.

blocks.raw: This is a strict liability offence, meaning intent or knowledge is not required for prosecution. The only defence is being able to demonstrate that your organisation had reasonable fraud prevention procedures in place at the time.
blocks.text: This is a strict liability offence, meaning intent or knowledge is not required for prosecution. The only defence is being able to demonstrate that your organisation had reasonable fraud prevention procedures in place at the time.

blocks.raw: 🏢 **Who’s Affected?**
blocks.text: 🏢 Who’s Affected?

blocks.raw: This applies to “large organisations”, defined as those meeting two or more of the following:
blocks.text: This applies to “large organisations”, defined as those meeting two or more of the following:

blocks.raw:
* More than 250 employees
* Annual turnover over £36 million
* Balance sheet total over £18 million
blocks.text: More than 250 employeesAnnual turnover over £36 millionBalance sheet total over £18 million

blocks.raw: It also applies to UK and overseas companies that carry on business in the UK.
blocks.text: It also applies to UK and overseas companies that carry on business in the UK.

blocks.raw: 🤝 **Who Counts as an “Associated Person”?**
blocks.text: 🤝 Who Counts as an “Associated Person”?

blocks.raw: This includes:
blocks.text: This includes:

blocks.raw:
* Employees
* Agents (such as consultants, intermediaries, or sales reps, **Modulr’s Partner clients could be considered agents of Modulr)**
* Subsidiaries
* Anyone performing services for or on behalf of the organisation
blocks.text: EmployeesAgents (such as consultants, intermediaries, or sales reps, Modulr’s Partner clients could be considered agents of Modulr)SubsidiariesAnyone performing services for or on behalf of the organisation

blocks.raw: ❗ **Why It Matters**
blocks.text: ❗ Why It Matters

blocks.raw: This offence is designed to shift the burden from investigating fraud after the fact to preventing it proactively. It’s a wake-up call for organisations to review their internal controls, training, and governance structures.
blocks.text: This offence is designed to shift the burden from investigating fraud after the fact to preventing it proactively. It’s a wake-up call for organisations to review their internal controls, training, and governance structures.

blocks.raw: **✅ What Should You Do to Prepare?**
blocks.text: ✅ What Should You Do to Prepare?

blocks.raw: The government’s guidance outlines six principles for “reasonable procedures”: top-level commitment, risk assessment, proportionate procedures, due diligence, communication and training, and monitoring and review.
blocks.text: The government’s guidance outlines six principles for “reasonable procedures”: top-level commitment, risk assessment, proportionate procedures, due diligence, communication and training, and monitoring and review.

blocks.raw:
1. Conduct a fraud risk assessment to identify where your organisation is most vulnerable.
2. Review and update internal policies to ensure they reflect the new legal requirements.
3. Implement proportionate prevention procedures tailored to your size, sector, and risk profile.
4. Train your people, especially those in high-risk roles or with decision-making authority.
5. Monitor and review your controls regularly to ensure they remain effective.

blocks.raw: ## Compliance in the News: Worldline
blocks.text: Compliance in the News: Worldline

blocks.raw: 🕵️‍♀️ **What Happened?**
blocks.text: 🕵️‍♀️ What Happened?

blocks.raw: A collaborative investigation by 21 European media outlets alleged that Worldline knowingly processed payments for high-risk clients involved in fraudulent activity.
blocks.text: A collaborative investigation by 21 European media outlets alleged that Worldline knowingly processed payments for high-risk clients involved in fraudulent activity.

blocks.raw:
**📉 Financial Impact**\
Following the publication of these reports, Worldline’s share price plummeted by over 40%, wiping out billions in market value in just one day. This has raised concerns about the company’s financial stability
blocks.text: 📉 Financial ImpactFollowing the publication of these reports, Worldline’s share price plummeted by over 40%, wiping out billions in market value in just one day. This has raised concerns about the company’s financial stability

blocks.raw:
**🧾 Worldline’s Response**\
Worldline has publicly reaffirmed its commitment to compliance, noting that it has:
blocks.text: 🧾 Worldline’s ResponseWorldline has publicly reaffirmed its commitment to compliance, noting that it has:

blocks.raw:
* Strengthened its merchant risk framework since 2023
* Terminated relationships with non-compliant clients
* Invested in fraud prevention and financial crime compliance
blocks.text: Strengthened its merchant risk framework since 2023Terminated relationships with non-compliant clientsInvested in fraud prevention and financial crime compliance

blocks.raw:
**⚠️ Why It Matters**\
This situation is a stark reminder of how quickly reputational and regulatory risks can translate into financial consequences. For organisations operating in or adjacent to the payments space, the Worldline case highlights the need for:
blocks.text: ⚠️ Why It MattersThis situation is a stark reminder of how quickly reputational and regulatory risks can translate into financial consequences. For organisations operating in or adjacent to the payments space, the Worldline case highlights the need for:

blocks.raw:
* Robust due diligence on clients and partners
* Transparent governance and escalation procedures
* Proactive fraud detection and AML controls
blocks.text: Robust due diligence on clients and partnersTransparent governance and escalation proceduresProactive fraud detection and AML controls

* Partners operating in similar sectors should be aware of the **potential for high-risk customers to attempt to migrate** from Worldline to other providers. Enhanced onboarding scrutiny and risk assessments are advised.

blocks.raw: ## Annual Audit & Compliance Fee Invoicing Change (Outsourced KYB / KYC Partners Only)
blocks.text: Annual Audit & Compliance Fee Invoicing Change (Outsourced KYB / KYC Partners Only)

blocks.raw: From the 1st July 2025 we are changing the way that we invoice the annual Audit & Compliance fee for Partners who have CDD responsibility for their Introduced Customers.
blocks.text: From the 1st July 2025 we are changing the way that we invoice the annual Audit & Compliance fee for Partners who have CDD responsibility for their Introduced Customers.

blocks.raw: Previously this fee was invoiced retrospectively once an audit had been completed. **The annual fee will now be invoiced during the month of anniversary of the contract commencement date.** This will make the process clearer and more streamlined for Partners.
blocks.text: Previously this fee was invoiced retrospectively once an audit had been completed. The annual fee will now be invoiced during the month of anniversary of the contract commencement date. This will make the process clearer and more streamlined for Partners.
